newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Peacekeepers face difficult task in Bosnia - Perry.
newsitem.headline: Peacekeepers face difficult task in Bosnia - Perry.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry warned on Thursday that the new international military force in Bosnia would face "a very difficult mission" next year and said civilian rebuilding of the country must advance quickly.

Perry ate a traditional Thanksgiving holiday lunch with U.S. and other troops at this U.S. base near Tuzla. He also met Russia's Deputy Defence Minister Vladimir Toporov and NATO officers to discuss the new 31,000-member force which will begin operating on December 20 and remain until mid-1998.

"We see the stabilisation force as facing a very difficult mission," Perry told reporters during a six-hour visit to Bosnia, saying tensions would be kept high by refugee resettlement and municipal elections in Bosnia as well as war crimes trials in The Hague.
The new NATO-led force, which will include 8,500 American and 1,200 Russian troops, is replacing a current 50,000-member peace implementation force (IFOR) which is currently leaving Bosnia.
"The peace we have currently in this land is pretty fragile. But it is still peace," said Toporov at a joint news conference with Perry.

The two men had lunch with U.S. Army General George Joulwan, commander of NATO forces in Europe, and with U.S., Russian and other troops on Perry's third successive Thanksgiving holiday visiting U.S. troops overseas.

"Happy Thanksgiving. This (visit) is my way and my country's way of saying thank you for your service," Perry told members of the U.S. First Infantry Division. I do not especially enjoy being away from home on Thanksgiving. But I always feel at home with our troops. I am proud of you."
Perry and Joulwan warned that the civilian rebuilding of Bosnia had moved too slowly and that it must be speeded up in order to bring a lasting peace between Moslems, Serbs and Croats in Bosnia.

"We expect these civilian agencies to gather momentum, to make more progress on economic recovery and rebuilding," Perry told reporters. "Because ultimately sustaining a peace in Bosnia depends on the success of those civilian operations."

Perry flew here from Naples, Italy, on the second leg of an eight-day globe-circling trip. He later left for Kuwait and will go to Qatar and Saudi Arabia and to Japan before returning home on December 4.

Perry said that the new "stabilisation force" (SFOR) will have the task of keeping a secure atmosphere in war-torn Bosnia in order to give civilian agencies a chance to do their work in a country where unemployment is over 75 per cent and ethnic hatred still runs deep.
"The civilian work has been, bluntly, slow to get off the ground. That is why you are (remaining) here," Perry told American troops.
Perry said on Wednesday that the new force, while operating under a U.N. mandate, would not guarantee peace and stability in the country.
"Fundamentally, the Bosnians themselves are going to have to make those changes," he said. "I think the key to whether they will want to do that is success in the economic restructuring."
